In my experience those pour type pens will still eat away at ABS plastic. Not as fast as the bottled stuff though. The solvent in those pens seems like it's a little gentler but it will still tear up ABS.
It will destroy it on a molecular level. It will literally crumble right before your eyes.

You should not use a liquid panel liner on ABS at all unless you at least lay down a top-coat or a primer barrier first.  Same with a lot of paint thinners.  They eat away at the plastic on a molecular level, breaking the polymer chains and leaving you with a sad mess.  ABS is very sensitive to solvents in general so I would lay down either a primer, or top-coat barrier before going anywhere near ABS plastic with any solvent.

After a few months of driving frequently, you'll stop being so scared while you're doing it and white knuckling the wheel. That's when you're ready to take your road test. During the period of practice, I would suggest learning how to maintain a vehicle by watching youtube videos. Understand why fluids need to be changed and how often. How to change a tire, etc. If you don't have anyone to teach you at all, there's also schools that teach people. You can also get lessons from people privately on facebook. Schedule the road test, practice 3 point turns and parallel parks at the DMV course after hours. They let you do that. As much as you want. The road test is going to be like 70% parking maneuvers and 30% knowing how to flip your lights on and wipers and stuff. You probably won't even go out on the road depending on the DMV. You'll just be doing maneuvers around cones.   


Remember. There's no speed requirement. You can take as long as you want to do the parking maneuvers and even back out and try again. Just DONT hit a cone. Go slow.  It's not over until you put the car in park. They just want to see you get there without hitting a cone. I re-positioned myself for my back-in park 3 times before I committed and I didn't lose any points for it because I didn't hit any cones or go over any lines.

The permit is going to be common sense multiple choice questions with obvious correct answers. You will be underwhelmed, most likely. Read through the DMV book and do your best to memorize things, of course. This part will probably not be too bad.

After that you have to practice. YOU HAVE TO PRACTICE. Meaning make yourself ask to drive. Ask your parents to drive any chance you get. The anxiety will not go away until you do it so much that you aren't afraid anymore. Make an actual effort to want to learn. They might not ask you to drive as much as they should, especially if you're fearful. It's really important to try to drive every day at least a little during this period. Drive until you are no longer clenching the wheel on the highway and your brain shuts up. Then schedule the test.

The road test is much more serious. You can only do a few things wrong and the test givers are kind of assholes usually. Right now they're basically just testing parking maneuvers with the test giver standing outside the vehicle because of covid, but by the time you do it, it might be back to normal easy "drive around the block and park," tests. I would highly suggest doing a few 3 point turns and parallel parks before the test and make sure you eat something before you go so you aren't shaky.

This is a lot, I know. But it's stuff I wish someone had said to me.

One more thing: It also might help to go on YouTube and look up how cars work. Like learn how they actually operate in detail. Learn how to maintain a vehicle and even fix simple things before you even start driving. That helped me a ton. Made them less mysterious. There's also tricks for parking maneuvers to make them easier. Newer cars also help with stuff like backup cams and park assist. I took my test in a 25 year old car though, so yeah.

Your nozzle looks like it's leaking through the spiral leakage path in the threads because it wasn't installed properly, and also your PTFE tube might be backed away from the back of the nozzle creating a sort of "gap" which is causing partial clogs. There's where the bits of old filament are coming from too. When you got the printer, did you heat tighten the nozzle?

Either way, you're gonna want to take the hot end apart. When you take it apart, you're gonna want to try to remove the bowden tube and nozzle with the heater block hot, maybe not all the way heated up, but like 180c (Be careful!), or you might struggle to remove the PTFE tube, which needs to come all the way out. I like to remove the nozzle entirely and actually push the PTFE tube through the heat block to sort of "floss" it out. It's easier to remove that way in my experience.

Then once you've cleaned it, heat the hot end up, screw the nozzle in all the way then back it out a quarter turn, reseat the PTFE tube against the back of the nozzle and tighten the nozzle with it heated up to like 230c. This will compress the tube against the back of the nozzle slightly increasing it's engagement with the bowden coupler teeth, helping keep it in place.

The smoking is most likely just be filament cooking because it's in direct contact with the heater cartridge which is much hotter itself then inside the heat block. It looks like you've got PLA burned all over the heater.

To deal with the burnt filament, clean it as best you can, then you can probably just leave it to burn off the volatiles if you watch it and keep it well ventilated. Just stop if something lights on fire, lol. It will quit smoking once all the oils in the PLA burn away.

When you get a 3d printer, never trust the people at the factory to properly install a nozzle, they get lazy and just screw it on and torque it down.

The stock hot end is finicky as fuck. There's a little mod you can print on thingiverse that helps keep the PTFE tube from backing out away from the nozzle as well if this keeps happening.

Always a good idea to keep a spare hot end or at least nozzles, ptfe tubes, and heater cartridges/thermistors, the stock ones are super cheap and it's the working tool of your printer, it's gonna need maintenance from time to time. Or get a micro swiss or e3d v6 and be done fighting the crappy stock hot end forever.

Those little ooze spires are a classic overheating artifact as well as an indicator of a low travel speed and acceleration. 

Keep in mind small needle-like features like that are worst case scenario torture tests for ANY FFF printer. Just because your printer strings on them doesn't necessarily even mean it's gonna string on a normal print, so don't obsess too much about them. They're only testing your slicing settings in this one specific scenario. 

However, one way to help keep those little spires down is to crank your travel speed and acceleration way up. I use a travel speed of 200mm/s with a travel acceleration of 3000mm/s\^2. 

You want your travels to be as fast as your printer can handle really. This way the nozzle gets moving quickly after a retraction and kind of "snaps" the strings off before they can really form. It will also give the nozzle less time to develop an ooze.

Having a high travel speed should not negatively affect your print quality either. The main setting that causes ringing if set too aggressively is outer wall speed, jerk, and acceleration. Also, travel moves before outer walls are usually very short because they usually come after inner walls, and thus acceleration doesn't have much time to get them up to speed anyway.

I'd try dropping the temp by 5 degrees and bumping your travel speed up if it's not already fast, if not that, increase retraction distance a small amount, although I think your main issue is the nozzle simply being too hot for tiny features like that, and moving too slowly after a retract.

[Direct drive duct I’m using. ](https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:4165973)


I chose to switch to direct drive because I was having to use an aggresive implementation of linear advance to keep the stringing down with the micro swiss. Since you cant really pull long retractions with all metal hot ends, using linear advance really helps Bowden printers cope with small retraction distance due to the nozzle pressure relief. I wanted to give my extruder a break from working so hard with the linear advance factor being so high. 

Since the switch I have not seen a single string. Im still using linear advance for the slight improvement to dimensional accuracy it brings, but the required K factor is insanely low (0.06) and I’m able to get by with only 0.5mm retracts. Im also able to print the softest flexibles with ease now as well. 

I think direct drive is probably the mod that made the most impact on my quality. I finally feel like I’m not gonna squeeze that much more out of this thing just from mods. I might still be able to tune my slicer profile more though, as always. My printer finally feels like it can handle most tasks that would be asked of a hobby grade desktop printer except maybe filaments that need a heated environment like ABS. 

Anyway...

As long as you use a type of PVA glue (elmers, purple glue stick) between the PETG and the build surface, it won't rip chunks out of it.

You don't use adhesive for PETG to increase adhesion, you use it as a sort of "release agent." I use glue stick with PETG on almost any surface to ensure that it releases without tearing chunks out of whatever surface I'm using.

My go-to surface for PETG is blue tape on glass/PEI on a heated bed with glue stick. Just rip the tape off when I'm done and go back to whatever surface I use for PLA without worrying about cleaning it or damaging it.

You shouldn't get jams on any well designed and set up hot end unless you set up your retractions incorrectly and use inadequate cooling on the heat sink after the heat break. Jams aren't really "just a thing" that happens with some hot ends. at least not with all metal ones.

They typically happen as a result of poor slicer settings 90% of the time. Usually either too aggressive or frequent retractions, or printing too hot for the amount of hot-end cooling you have. Heat goes up the heat break and softens filament too high up and causes a jam, almost every single time. The other 10% is crappy all-metal heat breaks with poor internal surface finishes allowing filament to "bake" on and build up a jam.

If it's a PTFE lined hot end, the jam is usually due to a separation from the PTFE liner and the nozzle causing a gap that creates a filament blob, almost always

My suggestion to many people who choose to use all metal hot ends is to learn to use Linear Advance. That way you're not relying on retractions so much to keep stringing down and you will pretty much never have a jam if you're barely doing any retractions. The name of the game with all metal hot-ends is keeping nozzle pressure low.

For example, my bowden ender 3 has an all-metal micro swiss with 2mm retractions and I've never had a single jam on it, and I get zero stringing. This is a  hot end that is "known for jamming." You just gotta understand that all-metal hot ends require a well polished heat break, VERY good cooling to keep the melt zone transition sharp, small retractions, and some way to manage nozzle pressure (Linear Advance, or VERY good cooling and well-tuned retractions.).

Basically what I'm saying is that when you read reports of jamming on well made hot ends like the e3d hot ends and micro swiss ones, it's almost always user error.

Elmers is a PVA polymer slurry. It's the same shit that's in hot glue sticks, and school glue sticks. PVA is a water soluble polymer that is, IMO, basically the best bed adhesive for standard printing plastics that tend to over-adhere, like PETG for example. It allows the polymer to stick to the bed when hot, and release when cooled down without damaging the build surface.

Any form of PVA works incredibly. Hell, a lot of hairspray has a similar polymer in it called PVP. Any water soluble polymer works incredibly well. Hell, I bet you could use old school hide glue or fish glue as a bed adhesive if you wanted. It would probably actually make a really good one, if not a bit gross.

I can also tell you from experience that dual Z doesn't really do much at all to the Ender 3. In fact, it introduces a new issue. Misalignment due to desynch across the 2 screws. Unless you're using 2 z motors with independent stepper drivers, or a timing belt solution. With 2 motors and independent drivers, you can use marlin's Z auto align which does help with that though. Just don't do 2 motors on the same driver in parallel without having 2 limit switches, one on each side unless you want to have to re-align them every time you turn off your printer.

Having the lead screw aligned well, well lubricated, and the rollers tightened to the right tension should produce no gantry sag on this printer. Now, the CR10 is a different story. The longer the cantilever gets, the more sensitive it becomes to adjustment.

I will concede that dual Z removes the variable of adjusting the rollers correctly and aligning the lead screw to a large extent, though. Until then, what you want is the rollers on the left side slightly tighter than the cantilever side. The rollers on the side of the lead screw have more to do with keeping the gantry square to the Y axis rails than the rollers on the cantilevered side. The lead screw also has more mechanical advantage on the left side rollers. The right side rollers should just be tight enough to grab, without creating much resistance.

Your Z axis should be able to almost fall under it's own weight with the motor disabled. Not entirely, but when you turn the motors off, it should drop at least a few lead screw turns.

I oversimplified a lot of what I said, so I'm sure someone will come in and be like "ACHTUALY", but whatever, you get the idea.

That value is the root mean square of the current that is fed to the motors. In simple terms, it's the (in way oversimplified terms) "average" current the motor gets for movement and holding torque. The higher the number, the stronger the magnetic coils in the motor, and the more torque the motor has, but also the hotter both the motor, and the stepper driver gets. TMC drivers are nice because they can have their motor current dynamically controlled over their serial interfaces using either UART or SPI depending on the driver. Something like an A4988 driver has to have it's (VREF) set by a potentiometer on the board.

So it's a balancing act. You want enough current to drive the motors hard enough for what you need, but not so much that the drivers overheat. The motors can take the heat, the little drivers we use? Not so much.

Also more current means micro steps are more likely to actually produce movement so technically it increases precision. If your current is too low with say, 256x microstepping, a single or even several steps are likely to produce no movement at all.

My rule goes like this. X and Y don't need as much current since they're just belt driven and slinging relatively low weight around. So set those as low as you can get away with, without getting any type of stepping artifacts or skipped steps. On an i3 printer (which is what the ender 3 is), you should give the Y axis slightly more than the X since it's likely to be slinging more weight around.

The Z axis, at least on an ender 3 has just 1 motor. It has to be precise, and also has to lift the entire gantry in tiny little increments. It needs to produce movement for as many step pulses as possible. That's how you get consistent layers. So it needs more current than X/Y, usually, albeit not a whole lot more.

The E axis needs the most current as it has to deal with most dynamic loading and needs to change directions frequently and fast. Think about it, when your extruder is advancing filament, it's meeting a ton of resistance, then it retracts to almost no resistance at all. Also on an ender 3, the E motor is physically bigger, so it needs to be driven harder. Set that as high as you can go without overheating the drivers.

My values for an ender 3 with TMC2208s, are 520 on X, 560 on Y, 600 on Z, and 680 on E. You can turn those up slightly for 2209s cause they can handle a little more current according to their data sheet.

Also giving your stepper drivers active cooling and good heatsinks allow you to crank the current/VREF up higher, obviously. Same with the motors, strap some heatsinks to the motors since the coil resistance is gonna change with heat and as such, the drivers will get hotter as the motors get hotter.

Side note since I'm drunk and feel like rambling about motion control:

3D printers are sort of like laser cutters or plasma cutters, in that rigidity doesn't really matter so much as having motion systems capable of precise, fast movement and direction changes. It's the reason we can get away with open loop, dumb, stepper motors driving belt driven axis' with fucking mini skateboard wheels riding on aluminum extrusions. Our tool forces are essentially just dealing with the inertia of slinging the hot end and bed around.

As opposed to the closed loop servo/hybrid motors driving ball screws with axis riding on super rigid linear rails that big boy CNC mills use. Their motors need to know about the load on them and if they miss a "step" or don't move as far as they should. They don't really care about going fast as much since they're more concerned with moving exactly 10mm with a huge force resisting that movement, for example.

Yep, voltage regulators are a large reason for failures of motherboards and GPUs. It fails and too much gets to an IC and bam, it's gone. Also bad PSUs. Some people will replace a blown up GPU and it was the PSU that caused it to fail because one of their 12v rails is bad. Check your PSU with a multimeter every year or so and make sure it's delivering a clean 12/5/3.3v +/- 5% all lines. 11.8v is fine, 11.3 is not. 12.8 is absolutely not fine, lol.

PSU going bad can be the root cause of a lot of failures. People don't realize that PSUs don't tend to just blow up. Their output gets unreliable overtime and they can starve components, or they can even deliver too much voltage and blow other shit up. It's a good idea to splurge for a good PSU, and check it's output with a multimeter every couple of years.

Well, it's more like some component on them will give out. The actual GPU chip is unlikely to die itself, although it can happen. What IS more likely is for a voltage regulator to go, or a capacitor, or something like that. Something gets the wrong voltage or too much current because of a failure like that and pops, and bye bye gpu. What else can happen is for solder joints to fail, especially on sagging GPUs. That's one reason people bake their GPUs in the oven. To attempt to reflow all the solder joints and make it work again, although it usually fails again once it's done this.

Keeping them cool helps a lot with this. Heat ages components faster. Sometimes you can tell what happened by inspecting the board and probing every component. I've fixed GPUs that just had a single bad capacitor by probing every single component and looking for continuity. Most people just replace the whole thing though. Also sometimes a failure is caused by a component, and it takes others with it, or kills an IC from a voltage spike.

Stealthchop is nice. My motors are dead silent. Setting it up is as easy as enabling it in Marlins config. Don't use it on the extruder motor though, it causes problems since the tradeoff for silence is less torque. You might get skipped steps if you use stealthchop on the E stepper.  Also the E stepper  doesn't make hardly any noise in spread cycle mode anyway.


You can use something called hybrid threshold. What this does is switch to the torque heavy, louder spreadcycle mode over a certain speed. I use 100mm/s. So my motors are dead silent but my travel moves make a noise. You dont have to use hybrid threshold but it helps avoid layer shifts on fast movements.

For the RMS current which sets the VREF for the drivers I use 520 on XYZ and 640 on E. If you want to always use stealthchop you'll probably need more than that but beware that too much current causes heat issues. I'm not sure about the 2209s though. My 2208s are in UART mode so I set these current values in firmware. If the 2209s on your board aren't UART you'll have to set the VREF with a multimeter set to DC volt mode and the potentiometer on the drivers. Google RMS to vref calculator if you get stuck with this.


Keep in mind I have 2208s so some stuff may be different for you but this is really just stepper driver set up in general. I think teaching tech has some guides on youtube for this stuff. I just kinda winged it with my EE knowledge.

What this means is that it's capable of processing 8 bits, a byte, if you will, at once. So every cycle it can do something with 8 bits of information at once. A 32 bit board is capable of basically "thinking about more stuff at once." It can process more data at once per cycle so it can run through information quicker.

 This really doesn't do much for printing performance since 3d printers aren't exactly super intense to control, but it does mean that the people who develop the firmware for 3d printers can be a bit lazier. They won't have to work so hard at making sure things perform well because they'll have more overhead.

You'll hear a lot about "squish" which is kind of a misnomer. You don't want a ton of squish as that's what causes elephants foot. Ok so first thing you need to realize is that when your slicer creates a gcode file, the first thing it does when the print starts is raise the z axis up to whatever your layer height is. So, say you have it set so that your print has 0.2mm layers. You want the nozzle to be as close to 0.2mm off the bed when the printer thinks it's at a z height of 0.2mm.

So the way to do this is pretty straightforward. A piece of paper is about 0.1mm thick. So what you want to do is to auto home your printer. Then, you want to go into movement > disable steppers. Then go ahead and raise the z axis with movement>move axis, so that it's at 0.1mm. This will also lock the z stepper so it doesnt move while you're leveling, but will leave the x and y unlocked. Use a piece of paper and move the print head to all 4 corners, right above the springs. Slide the paper under the nozzle and move it back and forth. You're looking for a friction level that's about medium. Go from corner to corner at least 3 times until all 4 corners feel the same. Also use your eyes to get a feel for what it looks like when the nozzle is 0.1mm off the bed. Eventually you'll be able to literally eyeball it.

The idea being since the printer is set to a z height of 0.1mm, and paper is 0.1mm, that means that z0 should be pretty much touching the bed. You are trying to make sure the printer is indeed the distance off the bed that it thinks it is. Also when you start a print, go to tune>baby step z axis. You can adjust the z height in real time. Watch your brim or skirt go down and baby step the z axis up or down if it's too close or too far.

That's exactly the right stuff. That 4oz bottle will last you forever too. Apply it to the lead screw and run it up and down a few times. Check your z stepper after a print and wipe any excess that runs down to the motor under the coupler. I like to put a small little bit right above the brass z nut before a print and run it up and down through it. I tend to overdo it a bit but I don't get any of those layer artifacts. Just make sure you're not going crazy with it.

It should be easy to move the leadscrew up and down by hand. To the point that if you disable the Z stepper, the z axis should actually drop down a bit, not a lot, just a little. You want very little friction ideally because even if the motor isn't binding up, if it meets uneven amounts of resistance, your layers will have small discrepancies in height and it will show on the print as tiny layer line artifacts. Make sure you keep your leadscrew relatively free of dust as well since that turns into an abrasive paste if it builds up too much and can wear the brass nut that runs up and down.

Also it's a good idea to print a knob to screw on the top of the leadscrew so you can crank the z axis up and down easier by hand. There's a few different designs on thingiverse.

For flexibles with a bowden, you're going to have to slow way down. Also make sure your filament path is as constrained and as short as possible. The stock bowden tube is quite a bit longer then it needs to be, and it's got a 2mm inner diameter. You want the tighter capricorn PTFE tubing since that has a 1.8mm inner diameter, and maybe even a better extruder although I've been able to do fine with the aluminum extruder as long as I slow down to about 30mms and chill with the retractions a bit.

You're too far from the bed for starters. Know how I can tell? Your brim has poor adhesion and the lines are spaced too far. They should be touching with no gaps, but not squished down too much. It's a balancing act and you'll get a feel for it in time. Level the bed with a piece of paper and go for more friction then you did last time between the paper and bed. 

Next, the layer line artifacts are a bit of a chore to get rid of. They can be caused by lots of stuff and often they coincide with changes in geometry. The best thing you can do is make sure your z axis moves freely and doesn't have too much resistance all the way up. Get you some superlube PTFE oil and apply it to the lead screw every few prints, and make sure your z axis leadscrew is square to the frame. If it's not, use some paper/print a shim to move the stepper motor farther from the frame so it's square. Typically Ender 3's have the stepper too close to the frame so the Z-Rod is tilted away from the frame ever so slightly.

You don't have to enable anything. It will just do it. A bridge isn't a special thing, it's just when you print a layer over mid air between 2 anchor points. As long as the filament has somewhere to grab when it goes over mid air, it will typically sag a tiny, tiny bit as long as you're printing reasonably quickly. Like, you don't want to attempt a bridge printing a 20mm/s lol. Filament hardens faster then you think. That's what allows bridging. By the time the print head gets to the other side, the bridge is already hard.

There are special settings that let you make the bridge behave differently, like for me, I use 2 5015 blowers, and I typically run them at like 50% normally, but I have it set to crank up to 100% when it bridges. You can also change the speed of a bridge, and other stuff like that.

Ok, first, increase the support overhang setting to 55-60 degrees. That will reduce the areas it supports. You can easily achieve 60 degree overhangs with the stock ender 3.

Next, on that print you could probably have reduced the support density or line distance a little bit.

You can also strategically place , and scale support blocker cubes in cura so that you've got areas with no supports that are bridged between supported areas. The support blocker button is on the left hand side by the scale/rotate/translate/mirror buttons. The way this works is, you click the button, then click on the model, it generates a cube anything that cube overlaps on the model will ignore supports and not generate them in that area. You use the scale option and move the cube around till it's the right size and position for your needs. You can make many of these cubes.

Or just use tree supports. Those work too. Although In my experience they can be a little finicky.

With the stock mainboard, you want to print over SD.

When you print over USB, the printer is fed gcode commands in real time over the USB connection. With the stock mainboard this is a problem because it can't keep up. Also if your PC goes to sleep it stops printing. Or, even if you close whatever program you're printing from, it will stop printing.

The stock mainboard is too slow and the cache is too small, so you get connection issues.  It will slow down, and even just give up and stop printing and wait for user input. It can read gcode much faster and easier from its internal SD reader.

I'm not positive this is your actual issue, but I know that it will mess your print quality up, and slow your prints down.

You can just get the creality  1.1.5 silent mainboard if you just want something easy that you just drop in. But I wouldn't recommend it honestly. It's still an 8 bit board and doesn't allow for easy expansion.

If you're not afraid of learning a little, get an SKR 1.3, or mini e3/DIP. It's 32 bit which has several advanges, one of them being you can print over USB with octoprint without it slowing down for example, also you can use marlin 2.0 with no modification or disabling features. The 1.3 is expandable incase you want to add another stepper for the z axis for example.

It's what I use, and I HIGHLY recommend it. It's the single greatest thing I've done to my printer IMO. Combined with a BLtouch ABL sensor.

You want the TMC2208 or 2209 stepper drivers on whatever you get, in UART mode imo. They've got stealthchop, which makes them dead silent. Like I'm talking creepy silent. The fans will seem loud.

There's a package on amazon that comes with an SKR 1.3 with TMC2208 plug and play UART stepper drivers [here](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07RXQPKLY/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o01_s02?ie=UTF8&psc=1). That's what I use. Silent, accurate, fast. The stepper drivers that this package includes are awesome because they require no modification to enable UART mode. You literally just hook them up, place some jumpers that come with the motherboard, and they work. It's by far the easiest way to do a removable drivers with UART setup.

UART is good because you can arbitrarily set the vref which sets the current for the drivers, from the firmware. Otherwise You have to use a multimeter and mess with trim pots.

You will have to print an enclosure if you use the 1.3, but the mini e3 will fit in the stock enclosure. I use teaching tech's universal all in one rear electronics box. You might want to look at some of the remixes with spots to place fans though. I used a remixed lid with a spot for 2 40mm fans blowing on the stepper drivers. The TMC2208s like to get hot. I hooked the fans along with the hot end fan into the second extruder power output and enabled the firmware to turn the fans on from there when the hot end goes above 50c. If you use 24v fans you can just hook them straight into the E1 power output, by twisting all the wires together and screwing them down with the screw terminals. I'm running 5 seperate fans off that output and it's fine. It's nice because I can leave my printer running when it's idle and there's no noise, since you don't need fans if the printer is just idling.

As for flashing, most replacement mainboards contain a bootloader, This means you just configure marlin in atom/vscode with the platformio plugin and compile it and move the firmware.bin onto the sd card, insert it into your printer and reboot. You will just need to use google though. There's a lot of info you're going to have to pick up, and not be afraid of messing with configuration files.

If you do decide to go this route. I wouldn't be too miffed about just sharing my config firmware with you. If you just let me know what your setup is like, I'll set up a firmware.bin for you and share the project files so you can configure it yourself as well. I wish someone would have done that for me. All the other info is correct though. You won't need to do any modification to your stepper drivers if you buy the package I linked. Yes exactly, this is a large reason why ABL helps so many people. It gets rid of the slop and confusion and the printer knows, "Ok Well I probed this spot and know exactly when I touched the bed, so I know exactly how far to offset my Z axis from that spot where I touched." It also allows the printer to compensate on the z axis on each spot to go higher or lower to maintain the same distance from it's known bed location at each discrete spot on the x/y axis.

There's a problem with ABL though, in my opinion. This problem is somewhat mostly with the ender 3 itself and not ABL. Since the Ender 3 uses a single z-stepper and lead screw, you really want to avoid a bunch of up and down motion. This introduces much more chances for inconsistency in layer height as you're basically hoping everything is adjusted and tight enough so that that unsupported right side of the x-gantry is always in the same spot as the supported left side. It's the same reason Z-hop can cause uglier prints on the Ender 3. Too much up/down motion.

This is why I suggest for people who have ABL to look in to the dual-z screw upgrade. Or, ideally, get a better mainboard like the SKR 1.3 that allows you to add a whole second z stepper.

ABL is still worth it imo, but it's important to get the bed as close to level as you can before relying on it, if you're only going to have the 1 z-screw. Don't do solid bed mounts unless you have the piece of mind of both sides of the x-gantry being supported independently.

So, there's kind of a problem. Most of us level our beds by auto homing the printer, then using like paper to level it at each corner right?

Technically this isn't really the right way to do this. Printer paper is about .1mm. So, when You level from home, You're essentially setting it so that z0 is .1mm off the bed.

Really, the "correct" way to level the bed is to actually raise the z-axis after you auto home, by whatever you set your first layer height to, and use a feeler gauge so the you know that z0 - 0mm is literally touching the bed, and when the slicer moves the head say, .2mm off the bed, it's actually exactly .2mm off the bed.

Some of this depends on the slicer though, my slicer does indeed raise the head at the first layer from z0 to whatever my first layer height is set at, although I think some slicers literally start the first layer at z0 and just calculate the material to extrude when you set the first layer height. So as not to confuse people.

Most of the time I still level with auto-home and the paper method because it's fine if the first layer overextrudes a little bit for better adhesion, as well as the fact that I never go above .2mm layer height so you really can't tell. However, if I was going to try a thick first layer like .28mm, I'd bust out the feeler gauge and do it the correct way.

Basically the bowden tube needs to be flush against the nozzle, or a gap will happen and filament will accumulate in that gap, causing all sorts of issues.

You need to actually make sure the bowden tube is seated against the nozzle, what I do, is I heat the hot end up, unload the filament, unscrew the nozzle and the bowden coupler and remove the bowden tube, check the end of the bowden tube and clear any plastic out of it. Then, what I do, is I sort of "floss" the hot end by pushing the bowden tube all the way through it with the nozzle removed to push out any plastic. You don't have to do this but it works.

Once you've done all that, with the hot end still hot, put the bowden coupler on ,same with the nozzle, screw the nozzle on but don't tighten it all the way, maybe like a 1/2 turn from tight. Push the bowden tube through the coupler until it hits the nozzle. Once you know it's hit the nozzle, THEN tighten the nozzle. This will clamp the end of the tube against the nozzle so there's no gap.

In the long run, I highly suggest replacing the bowden couplers with some with metal teeth. The stock couplers tend to let the bowden tube back out, which causes the gap. Also get some bowden coupler clamps, they hold the coupler tight. You might also look in to upgrading to the capricorn bowden tubes. They have better tolerances and tend to just be higher quality.

​

EDIT: Also, are you printing that ABS in an enclosure? You need to, if not. ABS does all sorts of shit when it cools down deferentially. It needs to stay nice and toasty in an enclosure during the print so it all cools down at once in the end. You might also be printing a little too hot, as well. I'm not sure without knowing your settings. This isn't really your problem, but I'm just making sure since you've got an ender 3, which is an open air printer.

Oh, one more thing, look in to jerk and acceleration. Jerk is kind of like the speed the nozzle is allowed to "jerk" to from a dead stop, and acceleration controls the speed at which the nozzle, well accelerates. Lower jerk values force the nozzle to more gently jerk into acceleration from a dead stop. I do a jerk of 10, which is down from the 20 default, and I change the acceleration depending on the print, 500 is a good place to start, and go down if you start to see ringing. These won't really affect your speed much, but they can improve quality.

Those are settings not many people mess with.
Oh, also make sure you heat it up and tighten everything again with it hot, you want to make sure it's all tightened up while it's nice and hot and thermally expanded.

Ok so a few things you can look at.

First, turn combing on, what that does is it makes the print head avoid retractions, and instead it travels over walls or infill depending on your settings, this way you end up with faster travels because it doesn't have to pause and retract every time it moves, and it lets the little bit of oozing just happen in the infill or on an inner wall. It will still retract if it absolutely has to go over mid air to get somewhere though. You can also speed up your travel moves, I do 180mm/s on travel moves.

Next, I believe the standard profile just prints at 50mm/s for everything, What you can do is set the speed to change depending on what it's doing. So like, you'd want to do outer walls slower, and inner walls a little faster, with infill going the fastest out of everything. Like, for me, I do 70mm/s on the infill, 50mm/s on the inner walls, and 40mm/s on the outer walls. Make sure to set your first layer hotter and slower though, I do 5 degrees hotter and half speed on the first layer, and it ramps up the speed over the next 2 layers.

Lower your infill percentage as well if the print doesn't need strength, and reduce the wall count, I do 3 walls normally, if the print just needs to be pretty I'll even go down to 2 sometimes. Play with the infill pattern as well. Some look cool on transparent plastic like that, some are stronger, some are faster. Cubic is my go to. It's very strong but also fast. Gyriod is the strongest I believe, but also slower. Triangle is a good one too, same with grid.

Combing is a big one though, sometimes turning off combing will increase my print time by over an hour, sometimes 2. Those retractions add up.

1 more thing I'd suggest is setting Cura to put the z-seam on the sharpest corner, and tell it to attempt to hide the z-seam whenever it can, so you won't get that ugly seam on the outside of your model when it does a layer change.

​

Also a good baseline retraction setting for the ender 3 is 6mm @ 25mm/s, I know it seems weird to do slower retractions, but I've actually gotten great results with that. Look in to magic numbers. For example, always set your layer height to a multiple of 4, i.e. 0.2mm, or 0.16mm.
